items.label: text
items.text: Electrons are constantly moving in the atom and it is impossible to know exactly where they are at any moment in time. You can only identify that they have a particular energy and that they are likely to be found in a certain region of space at some particular distance from the nucleus. Electrons with different energies are found at different distances from the nucleus. items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: The atomic number defines an element and is unique to that element. We can identify an element by its atomic number instead of its name. We could talk about a wristwatch made from the element with atomic number 79 instead of talking about 'a gold wristwatch', or say that the element with atomic number 17 is poisonous instead of saying 'chlorine is poisonous'. However, these are more complicated ways of describing things!

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE STRUCTURE OF THE ATOM

items.label: text
items.text: Atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons. These particles are sometimes called sub-atomic particles because they are smaller than an atom.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 3.4 The structure of a helium atom

items.label: text
items.text: The nucleus of the atom contains protons and neutrons, and is shown highly magnified in Figure 3.4. In reality, if you scale up a helium atom to the size of a sports hall the nucleus would be no more than the size of a grain of sand.

items.label: text
items.text: The relative masses and charges of protons, neutrons and electrons are shown in Table 3.1.

items.label: table
items.text:
Table 3.1 The properties of protons, neutrons and electrons

| Particle   | Relative mass   |   Relative charge |
|------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| proton     | 1               |                +1 |
| neutron    | 1               |                 0 |
| electron   | 1/1836          |                -1 |

items.label: caption
items.text: Table 3.1 The properties of protons, neutrons and electrons

items.label: text
items.text: Virtually all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus because electrons have a much smaller mass than protons and neutrons.

items.label: text
items.text: The masses and charges are measured relative to each other because the actual values are incredibly small. For example, it would take about 600 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 (6 × 1023) protons to weigh 1 g.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ATOMIC NUMBER AND MASS NUMBER

items.label: text
items.text: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus is called its atomic number or proton number. Each of the118 different elements has a different number of protons. For example, if an atom has 8 protons it must be an oxygen atom:

items.label: text
items.text: atomic number = number of protons

items.label: text
items.text: The mass number (sometimes known as the nucleon number) counts the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of the atom: mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons
